passage: When I was nine, Papa promised, “I'll be at your recital, Preeti, front row.” I practised for weeks. On the day, his seat stayed empty, and I played badly. He came in later, breathless, saying the train was late. I said I was fine, but my chest felt heavy, and I didn't want to hug him. That night he sat on my bed and said, “I'm sorry. I broke my promise, and I understand why you're hurt. I'll tell you honestly next time if I can't make it.” I remember his voice. It didn't fix the day, but I trusted him more because he was honest.

qa.q: What did Papa promise?
qa.a: To be at the recital in the front row.

qa.q: How did the writer feel when the seat stayed empty, and how was it shown?
qa.a: The writer felt hurt and sad, shown by a heavy chest and not wanting to hug Papa, even though saying everything was fine.

qa.q: What did Papa do that started to repair the trust?
qa.a: He apologised for breaking his promise, said he understood the hurt and promised to be honest next time.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt sitting on the bed that night?
qa.a: He was probably sorry and worried, since he explained honestly and promised to do better. 🤍

grounding: A child treats a broken pledge as a serious hurt, and an adult builds trust by keeping promises or explaining honestly.

passage: Counsellor's note. Nazia told me today that her mother promised to pick her up early every Friday. For three Fridays her mother was late. Nazia spoke quietly, and she twisted her school tie. She said, “I stopped believing when she says it.” I asked what she wanted. She said she wanted her mother to say honestly if she cannot come. With her permission I spoke to her mother, Mrs. Shreya. Mrs. Shreya said she had not realised how much it mattered. She will tell Nazia in advance when she cannot come. I will check in with Nazia next week. Ms. Sharma.

qa.q: How many Fridays was Nazia's mother late?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What did Nazia's twisting of her tie and quiet voice suggest, and what did she say she wanted?
qa.a: They suggested she felt hurt and worried her mother's promises meant nothing, and she said she wanted her mother to say honestly if she cannot come.

qa.q: What is Mrs. Shreya going to do differently?
qa.a: She will tell Nazia in advance when she cannot come.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Shreya have felt when she learned how much it mattered?
qa.a: She had not realised, so she was probably surprised and sorry, and willing to change.

grounding: A child treats a broken promise as a hurt, and honest explanation from an adult builds trust.

passage: Friday. Asif's diary. Abbu promised last week, “I'll be at your race, no matter what.” This morning he called from the office. His voice was sad. “Beta, the machine at work broke and I'm the only one who can fix it. I can't come. I'm really sorry. I know I promised.” I felt like someone had let the air out of me. I said, “You PROMISED,” and hung up. Then I felt bad. At the race, Gurpreet's mum filmed me running, for Abbu. I came second. Tonight Abbu watched the video three times and said, “Next time I promise, I'll only promise what I can control.” That made it a bit better.

qa.q: Why couldn't Abbu come to the race?
qa.a: The machine at work broke, and he was the only one who could fix it.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when Abbu said he couldn't come?
qa.a: Asif felt deflated and hurt, as if the air had been let out, because Abbu had promised.

qa.q: How did Abbu handle the broken promise?
qa.a: He called beforehand, explained honestly and said sorry, then watched the video and promised to only promise what he can control.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet's mum help?
qa.a: She filmed Asif's race so Abbu could still see it, which softened the disappointment.

grounding: Shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and honest explanation helping rebuild trust.

passage: Before leaving for the district town, Rekha knelt in the courtyard and held Yamini's hands. “I promise I'll be back before dark to see your dance at the school function.” Yamini had heard promises before, from other grown-ups. That afternoon the rain came down in sheets, and the last bus from town was cancelled. Yamini stood at the school gate in her costume, watching the empty road. The function began. Her turn came closer. Then, just as her music started, a figure came splashing up the path, sari soaked to the knees, chappals in one hand. Rekha had walked four kilometres. She stood at the back, dripping, and waved. Yamini danced better than she ever had.

qa.q: How far did Rekha walk?
qa.a: Rekha walked four kilometres.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she watched the empty road?
qa.a: Yamini felt anxious and doubtful, afraid the promise would be broken like other grown-ups' promises before.

qa.q: Why did Rekha's kept promise matter so much?
qa.a: Keeping it despite the rain and cancelled bus showed Yamini her mother's word could be trusted.

qa.q: What might the walk have been like for Rekha?
qa.a: It was probably wet and exhausting, but she was determined to keep her promise to Yamini.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a parent's pledge and a kept promise building trust.

passage: In their Stockholm flat, Astrid had promised Kaito a trip north to see the northern lights in the winter holiday. He'd drawn them on every page of his notebook. Two days before, she sat on his bed. “Kaito, I have to tell you something honestly. My work has changed my holiday, and we can't go this year. I'm really sorry. I know I promised.” Kaito turned to the wall. “You always say sorry.” Astrid didn't argue. “You're right to be upset. A promise is serious.” She took out the calendar. “February, the weekend after your birthday. I've already asked for the days off. It's written here, in pen.” Kaito looked at the pen mark for a long time, then nodded.

qa.q: When is the new trip planned?
qa.a: It's planned for February, the weekend after Kaito's birthday.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when he turned to the wall?
qa.a: Kaito felt hurt and let down, because he had been dreaming of the trip and a promise was broken.

qa.q: How did Astrid handle breaking the promise?
qa.a: She told him honestly and early, accepted his upset and made a specific new plan with the days already booked.

qa.q: What might Astrid have felt telling Kaito?
qa.a: Astrid probably felt guilty and sad, knowing how much the trip meant to him.

grounding: Shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and honest explanation and a firm new plan rebuilding trust.

passage:
All morning at the school sports day, Ganga kept checking the gate. Papa had said, "I promise. I'll be there for your relay, front row."

The relay started. The front row had Pooja's mother and Mariam's grandfather, but no Papa. Ganga ran her leg fast, handed on the baton, then sat under the tree and wouldn't eat her lunch.

At four, Jomon came through the gate, still in his hospital porter's uniform. He sat down beside her. "I broke my promise, and I'm sorry. They called me in for an emergency shift, and I couldn't get away. I should have phoned the school office to tell you."

Ganga didn't look at him. "You PROMISED."
"I know. Next time I'll only promise what I'm sure of."

qa.q: What was Jomon still wearing when he arrived?
qa.a: His hospital porter's uniform.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she sat under the tree and wouldn't eat?
qa.a: Deeply hurt and let down that Papa broke his promise to be in the front row.

qa.q: What did Jomon do that could help rebuild Ganga's trust?
qa.a: He apologised, explained honestly why he couldn't come, admitted he should have phoned, and promised to promise only what he is sure of.

qa.q: What was it like for Jomon to face Ganga's "You PROMISED"?
qa.a: Jomon knows he let her down, and he accepts her anger instead of arguing, which shows he takes the broken promise seriously.

grounding: It shows a child treating a parent's broken promise as a serious hurt, and the parent explaining honestly to rebuild trust.
